sources.entry: Instruction-Based Sampling: A New Performance Analysis Technique - Defines skid, why a sample lands after the culprit, and how tagging one op through the pipeline removes it.

summary.title: Instruction-Based Sampling: A New Performance Analysis Technique for AMD Family 10h Processors
summary.one_liner: Learn why classic performance-counter sampling misattributes events to nearby instructions (skid) and how AMD's Instruction-Based Sampling tags one op or fetch to pinpoint the true culprit instruction.
takeaways: Performance counter samples report an instruction pointer that can be many instructions (up to 72) away from the culprit, because of skid from out-of-order execution and in-order retirement.
IBS tags a selected fetch or op and follows it through the pipeline, so events are attributed to the instruction that caused them.
IBS op sampling reports per-op data such as branch misprediction, cache and TLB misses, miss latency, and local vs remote memory access in a single run.
In the matrix multiplication example, IBS pinpointed the cache and DTLB misses to the fmul at 0x4011C2, which PMC sampling had spread across neighboring instructions.
summary.summary: This 2007 AMD technical note by Paul Drongowski introduces Instruction-Based Sampling (IBS) for AMD Family 10h (Barcelona) processors. It first shows how conventional performance counter sampling suffers from skid, using a textbook matrix multiplication program (simple_classic) as a worked example. It then explains IBS fetch sampling and op sampling, which tag one operation and monitor it through the pipeline, and compares the resulting per-instruction tables with the PMC results. It closes with notes on data-centric NUMA analysis and profile-directed compiler optimization, and points to AMD CodeAnalyst and the Family 10h optimization guide.
